Geospatial Analytics for Peace

Take-home Exercise 2

Author

Zhiyi Hao

Published

October 4, 2026

Modified

October 23, 2026

1 Introduction

1.1 Study context

This report studies recorded armed conflict events in Myanmar from 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025. The spatial unit is the township and the main time unit is the month.

Myanmar’s post-2021 conflict involves geographically uneven interactions among the military, resistance organisations, ethnic armed organisations, and civilian communities. Township-level analysis cannot explain these relationships by itself, but it can identify where recorded violence forms unusual local concentrations and where those concentrations change through time.

1.2 Research questions and objectives

The analysis asks:

  1. Where do recorded conflict events form significant local clusters or spatial outliers?
  2. Which township-level hot spot patterns persist, emerge, intensify, or weaken through time?

The objectives are to prepare an analysis-ready township-month dataset, identify significant local clusters and spatial outliers, trace monthly hot spot movement, classify changing hot spots, and translate the findings into cautious peace-building priorities.

1.3 Analytical workflow

Stage Purpose Main output
Data preparation Link ACLED events to stable MIMU township P-codes and audit data quality Township-level event table
Space-time construction Retain every township-month combination, including observed zero-event months Complete monthly space-time cube
Descriptive analysis Establish the spatial and temporal distribution of recorded events Choropleth maps and monthly trend
Local spatial analysis Detect clusters and compare hotspot composition across conflict dimensions Local Moran’s I, local Gi*, and hotspot-agreement maps
Emerging Hot Spot Analysis Evaluate temporal trends in monthly local Gi* values Mann-Kendall results and EHSA classes

The workflow follows the course sequence in Chapters 10 and 11, with the Chapter 6 small-multiple design adapted for monthly comparison. Each analytical section states the neighbourhood definition, statistical decision rule, interpretation, and limitation.

NoteReading the results

The results describe the geography of recorded events. They do not measure all violence, population risk, or causal effects. A significant result is interpreted under the selected township boundaries, monthly time bins, neighbourhood rule, and permutation model.

2 Analytical framework

2.1 Local spatial association

Local Moran’s I distinguishes clusters of similar values from spatial outliers, while Getis-Ord Gi* identifies local concentrations of high values. Stankov et al. (2017), Arif and Purnomo (2017), and Fergen and Bergstrom (2021) demonstrate how these measures reveal local geographical inequality that a global summary can conceal. Khan et al. (2017) also show how local statistics can locate significant geographical concentrations.

2.2 Space-time analysis

EHSA combines a sequence of local Gi* statistics with the Mann-Kendall trend test. Putrenko, Pashynska, and Nazarenko (2018) motivate the use of space-time cubes for event data. Boschan and Roman (2024) and Kim and Lee (2023) show how EHSA separates new, consecutive, persistent, sporadic, and oscillating hot spots, allowing interventions to respond to temporal behaviour rather than a single-period concentration.

2.3 Conflict interpretation

Mack and Kam (2018) frame political violence as a spatio-temporal knowledge-discovery problem and give particular attention to violence against civilians. Tan and Kam (2019) demonstrate the value of comparing related variables and geographical profiles rather than relying on one aggregate map. These studies support interpreting the results as recorded spatial patterns while avoiding unsupported causal claims.

3 Data and study design

3.1 Data sources

The aspatial data are the ACLED Myanmar event export supplied for this exercise. The spatial data are Myanmar township boundaries from the MIMU GeoNode, Admin 3, P-code version 9.4.

Dataset Role Spatial or temporal detail Source
ACLED Myanmar events Event dates, types, coordinates, fatalities, and source fields Event points, 1 January 2021 to 30 September 2025 Exercise data supplied through eLearn
MIMU township boundaries v9.4 Stable township geometry and P-code key 330 Admin-3 township polygons MIMU GeoNode

The raw files are kept separately:

  • data/aspatial/raw/ACLED_Data_Myanmar_Jan2021-Sep2025.csv
  • data/geospatial/raw/myanmar_townships_mimu_v9_4.geojson

The MIMU township boundary layer has 330 polygon features. ACLED records are event-level observations, so the final analytical table is created by linking events to the township polygons and then aggregating by township and month.

The preparation stage derives four township-month variables. event_count is the primary variable in the current LMSA and EHSA workflow; the remaining measures preserve substantively different dimensions for comparison and sensitivity analysis.

Derived variable Definition Analytical meaning
event_count Number of recorded ACLED events Overall recorded conflict activity
fatality_count Sum of reported fatalities Reported lethal burden, subject to missingness and reporting uncertainty
battle_count Number of events classified as Battles Armed confrontation activity
civilian_count Number of events classified as Violence against civilians Directly recorded civilian-targeting activity

3.2 Packages and setup

The packages are limited to the tasks required by the workflow. Listing their roles makes the computational dependencies and the reason for each dependency visible.

Package Purpose in this exercise
pacman Load all required packages through one reproducible setup call
sf Import, validate, transform, join, and map event points and township polygons
sfdep Construct neighbours and weights; compute Local Moran’s I, local Gi*, space-time objects, and EHSA
spdep Diagnose connected components in the spatial neighbour graph
tmap Produce the thematic maps used to communicate spatial results
tidyverse Import, clean, aggregate, join, reshape, and visualise tabular data
lubridate Parse event dates and create regular monthly time bins
Kendall Perform the Mann-Kendall trend test on township Gi* sequences
scales Format axes and numerical labels
knitr Present compact analytical tables in the Quarto report

set.seed(626) is used before permutation-based procedures so that simulated results can be reproduced.

4 Data quality and spatial matching

4.1 Clean the event fields

Show code 
acled <- acled_raw %>%
  transmute(
    event_id = event_id_cnty,
    event_date = as.Date(event_date),
    year = as.integer(year),
    time_precision = as.integer(time_precision),
    country,
    admin1 = na_if(str_squish(admin1), ""),
    admin2 = na_if(str_squish(admin2), ""),
    admin3 = na_if(str_squish(admin3), ""),
    location = na_if(str_squish(location), ""),
    event_type,
    sub_event_type,
    civilian_targeting,
    latitude = as.numeric(latitude),
    longitude = as.numeric(longitude),
    geo_precision = as.integer(geo_precision),
    fatalities = as.numeric(fatalities),
    source
  ) %>%
  filter(
    country == "Myanmar",
    event_date >= as.Date("2021-01-01"),
    event_date <= as.Date("2025-09-30")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    month = floor_date(event_date, unit = "month"),
    admin1_key = str_remove_all(str_to_lower(admin1), "[^a-z0-9]"),
    admin3_key = str_remove_all(str_to_lower(admin3), "[^a-z0-9]")
  )

The event count is the main measure because it is available for every event. Fatalities are retained as a secondary measure, but missing fatality values are not silently changed into a claim of zero deaths. The precision table makes ACLED’s temporal and geographic coding uncertainty visible before aggregation.

TipMy observation

The filtered file is large and mostly complete for date and coordinates: 87,103 records remain in the study period, with no duplicate event IDs and no missing coordinates. The main quality issue is the 1,112 missing ACLED township names. I therefore use the MIMU coordinate join as the analytical key and keep the original ACLED names for comparison. This follows ACLED’s advice to treat event records and administrative labels as fields that still need checking.

4.3 Match events to MIMU townships

The supplied ACLED file does not contain MIMU P-codes. I use the coordinates to assign each event to a MIMU township polygon, then compare the assigned township with the ACLED admin3 field. This creates a reproducible P-code key and also exposes records that need checking.

Show code 
event_points <- acled %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

data_preparation_summary <- tibble(
  stage = c(
    "Raw ACLED records",
    "Records in the study period",
    "Records converted to spatial points"
  ),
  records = c(
    nrow(acled_raw),
    nrow(acled),
    nrow(event_points)
  )
)

kable(data_preparation_summary)
stage records
Raw ACLED records 87109
Records in the study period 87103
Records converted to spatial points 87103
Show code 
event_points_matched <- st_join(
  event_points,
  townships %>% select(TS, TS_PCODE),
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

event_table <- event_points_matched %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(
    mimu_ts_key = str_remove_all(str_to_lower(TS), "[^a-z0-9]"),
    name_check = case_when(
      is.na(TS_PCODE) ~ "unmatched spatially",
      is.na(admin3) ~ "admin3 missing; spatial match retained",
      admin3_key == mimu_ts_key ~ "name agrees",
      admin3 == "Pangsang" & TS == "Pangsang (Panghkam)" ~ "known name variant",
      TRUE ~ "name needs review"
    )
  )

event_table %>%
  count(name_check, sort = TRUE) %>%
  kable()

Spatial match Records Share (%)
Matched to a MIMU township 87094 99.99

The spatial match is the key transition from event-level data to township-level analysis. Records without a township P-code remain in the audit, but they are excluded from township aggregation rather than assigned by guesswork.

Only events with a valid MIMU township P-code enter township-level spatial analysis. Unmatched records remain visible in the quality table and are not silently assigned.

NoteMy observation

Most records agree with the MIMU township name. The 1,112 records with missing ACLED admin3 are still spatially usable, while 9 points fall outside the township polygons and 7 name mismatches need review. This is why I do not join by text alone. The coordinate-to-P-code join is the stronger link for the cube, and the exceptions remain visible instead of being silently forced into a township.

5 Aggregation and the space-time cube

5.1 Build a complete township-month table

The aggregation follows the time-cube logic used in the course exercises. I define the spatial and temporal grain first, count events, and then complete every township-month combination. A missing combination therefore becomes an observed zero, not an unknown value.

Show code 
months <- seq(
  as.Date("2021-01-01"),
  as.Date("2025-09-01"),
  by = "month"
)

event_counts <- event_table %>%
  filter(!is.na(TS_PCODE)) %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE, month) %>%
  summarise(
    event_count = n(),
    fatality_count = sum(fatalities, na.rm = TRUE),
    battle_count = sum(event_type == "Battles", na.rm = TRUE),
    civilian_count = sum(
      event_type == "Violence against civilians",
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

township_month <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  TS_PCODE = townships$TS_PCODE,
  month = months
) %>%
  left_join(event_counts, by = c("TS_PCODE", "month")) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(event_count, fatality_count, battle_count, civilian_count),
      ~ replace_na(.x, 0)
    )
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    townships %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST, DT),
    by = "TS_PCODE"
  ) %>%
  arrange(TS_PCODE, month)

township_month %>%
  summarise(
    townships = n_distinct(TS_PCODE),
    months = n_distinct(month),
    rows = n(),
    zero_event_bins = sum(event_count == 0),
    missing_event_counts = sum(is.na(event_count))
  ) %>%
  kable()
townships months rows zero_event_bins missing_event_counts
330 57 18810 7695 0
Show code 
cube_check <- township_month %>%
  count(TS_PCODE) %>%
  summarise(
    minimum_months = min(n),
    maximum_months = max(n),
    expected_months = length(months)
  )

kable(cube_check)
minimum_months maximum_months expected_months
57 57 57
NoteWhat this means

The complete cube has 330 townships and 57 monthly slices, so every township has the same time support. Zero-event township-months are retained as zeros. This matters because Emerging Hot Spot Analysis needs a regular sequence; dropping quiet months would turn the absence of recorded events into missing data and would bias temporal comparisons.

5.2 Create the space-time cube

Show code 
conflict_st <- spacetime(
  township_month,
  townships_proj,
  .loc_col = "TS_PCODE",
  .time_col = "month"
)

is_spacetime_cube(conflict_st)
[1] TRUE

The cube has one regular monthly series for every township. This structure is required before calculating the time sequence of local Gi* values.

6.2 Monthly pattern

Show code 
monthly_totals <- township_month %>%

  summarise(

The time series is used to identify broad changes in recorded event volume. It does not replace the township-level analysis because national totals can hide local changes in where events occur.

TipMy observation

The monthly curve gives the background rhythm of recorded conflict activity. A high month does not mean every township was high at the same time. This is the reason for keeping the local monthly Gi* sequence rather than interpreting the national total alone. It follows the space-time cube logic used by Kim and Lee (2023).

7 Local Measures of Spatial Association

7.1 Queen neighbours and row-standardised weights

The first local analysis follows Chapter 10. Queen contiguity defines neighbours that share either a boundary or a vertex. Row-standardised weights give each township’s neighbours a comparable total influence.

Show code 
township_weights <- township_totals %>%
  mutate(
    nb = st_contiguity(geometry),
    wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1
  )

neighbour_summary <- tibble(
  township = township_weights$TS,
  neighbours = lengths(township_weights$nb)
) %>%
  summarise(
    minimum_neighbours = min(neighbours),
    median_neighbours = median(neighbours),
    maximum_neighbours = max(neighbours),
    zero_neighbour_units = sum(neighbours == 0),
    connected_components = spdep::n.comp.nb(township_weights$nb)$nc
  )

kable(neighbour_summary)
minimum_neighbours median_neighbours maximum_neighbours zero_neighbour_units connected_components
1 5 11 0 4
NoteMethod note

Queen contiguity is the same neighbour idea used in the course local-measures workflow: shared edges or vertices. The network has 4 connected components and 0 zero-neighbour township(s). The disconnected components arise from Myanmar’s separated coastal and island geometries. Local statistics operate within these components, so no neighbourhood influence is assumed across the gaps.

7.2 Local Moran’s I

Show code 
set.seed(626)

lisa <- township_weights %>%
  mutate(
    local_moran = local_moran(
      event_count,
      nb,
      wt,
      nsim = 99,
      sample_Ei = FALSE,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    ),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(local_moran) %>%
  mutate(
    p_ii_sim_fdr = p.adjust(p_ii_sim, method = "BH"),
    LISA_cluster = case_when(
      is.na(p_ii) ~ "Insignificant",
      p_ii < 0.05 ~ as.character(mean),
      TRUE ~ "Insignificant"
    ),
    LISA_cluster = factor(
      LISA_cluster,
      levels = c(
        "Insignificant",
        "Low-Low",
        "Low-High",
        "High-Low",
        "High-High"
      )
    )
  )

lisa %>%
  count(LISA_cluster, sort = TRUE) %>%
  kable()
LISA_cluster n geometry
Insignificant 292 MULTIPOLYGON (((9009253 178…
High-High 34 MULTIPOLYGON (((9170405 265…
Low-High 4 MULTIPOLYGON (((9426095 223…
Show code 
lisa_significance <- tibble(
  significance_rule = c(
    "Analytical p-value (course baseline)",
    "Permutation p-value",
    "BH-adjusted permutation p-value"
  ),
  significant_townships = c(
    sum(lisa$p_ii < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lisa$p_ii_sim_fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

kable(lisa_significance)
significance_rule significant_townships
Analytical p-value (course baseline) 38
Permutation p-value 67
BH-adjusted permutation p-value 0
WarningMultiple-testing resolution

With 99 permutations, the smallest attainable simulated p-value is approximately 1 / (99 + 1) = 0.01. A Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across 330 townships starts from a threshold of 0.05 / 330, which is smaller than the permutation resolution. The zero BH-adjusted count therefore reflects both multiple-testing control and limited simulation resolution. The course-required nominal p < 0.05 map is retained, and its clusters are treated as screening evidence rather than definitive discoveries.

Show code 
tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(
    "LISA_cluster",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
      values = c(
        "grey85",
        "#2166AC",
        "#67A9CF",
        "#EF8A62",
        "#B2182B"
      )
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA cluster")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(states_proj) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.9) +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I clusters (p < 0.05)")

High-High and Low-Low are local clusters. High-Low and Low-High are spatial outliers. Insignificant townships remain visible as context and are not interpreted as clusters.

TipMy observation

The course-baseline LISA result contains 34 High-High townships and 4 Low-High outliers under the analytical p-value. The permutation and BH-adjusted counts are reported separately because they answer the same question under stricter reference distributions. High-High indicates neighbouring high recorded counts; it does not establish one continuous conflict process.

7.3 Local Gi*

Chapter 10 defines Gi* neighbours with a critical fixed-distance band and explicitly includes each township itself. The critical threshold is the largest first-nearest-neighbour distance, ensuring that every township has at least one neighbour. This construction differs from the Queen weights retained for Local Moran’s I.

Show code 
set.seed(626)

critical_distance <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(township_totals))

gistar_weights <- township_totals %>%
  mutate(
    nb = include_self(
      st_dist_band(geometry, upper = critical_distance)
    ),
    wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1
  )

gistar <- gistar_weights %>%
  mutate(
    gistar = local_gstar_perm(
      event_count,
      nb,
      wt,
      nsim = 99,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    ),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gistar) %>%
  mutate(
    p_sim_fdr = p.adjust(p_sim, method = "BH"),
    hotspot_class = case_when(
      p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
      p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
      TRUE ~ "Not significant"
    ),
    hotspot_class = factor(
      hotspot_class,
      levels = c("Not significant", "Cold spot", "Hot spot")
    )
  )

gistar %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(hotspot_class, sort = TRUE) %>%
  kable()
hotspot_class n
Cold spot 148
Not significant 104
Hot spot 78
Show code 
gistar_diagnostics <- tibble(
  critical_distance_km = critical_distance / 1000,
  minimum_neighbours = min(lengths(gistar_weights$nb)),
  median_neighbours = median(lengths(gistar_weights$nb)),
  maximum_neighbours = max(lengths(gistar_weights$nb))
)

kable(gistar_diagnostics, digits = 1)

  hot_spots = c(
    sum(gistar$p_sim < 0.05 & gistar$gi_star > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(gistar$p_sim_fdr < 0.05 & gistar$gi_star > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  ),
  cold_spots = c(
    sum(gistar$p_sim < 0.05 & gistar$gi_star < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(gistar$p_sim_fdr < 0.05 & gistar$gi_star < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

) %>%

  tm_polygons(
    "hotspot_class",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
      values = c("grey88", "#2166AC", "#B2182B")
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Gi* class")
  ) +

Local Moran’s I identifies similarity or contrast between a township and its neighbours. Gi* focuses here on statistically significant concentrations of high values. The two maps answer related but different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable.

TipMy observation

The fixed-distance Gi* result contains 78 hot spots and 148 cold spots at nominal p < 0.05. The critical distance is 185.8 km and the median township has 60 neighbours including itself. Cold spots satisfy the assignment’s overall spatial screening objective. The remaining analysis concentrates on high-value clusters because they are the direct conflict-priority question. The broad fixed-distance support can smooth local differences, while the monthly Queen model reveals change among immediately adjacent townships.

7.4 Do conflict dimensions point to the same places?

The aggregate count can hide whether a hotspot reflects armed confrontation, direct violence against civilians, or both. The next comparison holds the Queen neighbourhood, permutation count, and significance threshold constant, changing only the conflict variable. This makes differences across the three maps substantively interpretable.

Show code 
set.seed(626)

dimension_variables <- tibble(
  dimension = c("All events", "Battles", "Violence against civilians"),
  variable = c("event_count", "battle_count", "civilian_count"),
  key = c("all_events", "battles", "civilian_violence")
)

dimension_nb <- include_self(
  st_contiguity(st_geometry(township_totals))
)
dimension_wt <- st_weights(
  dimension_nb,
  style = "W",
  allow_zero = TRUE
)

dimension_gistar <- pmap_dfr(
  dimension_variables,
  function(dimension, variable, key) {
    local_gstar_perm(
      township_totals[[variable]],
      dimension_nb,
      dimension_wt,
      nsim = 99,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    ) %>%
      transmute(
        TS_PCODE = township_totals$TS_PCODE,
        dimension,
        key,
        gi_star,
        p_sim,
        is_hotspot = p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0,
        hotspot_status = factor(
          if_else(is_hotspot, "Hot spot", "Not a hot spot"),
          levels = c("Not a hot spot", "Hot spot")
        )
      )
  }
)

dimension_gistar %>%
  count(dimension, hotspot_status) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = hotspot_status,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  kable()

All events 306 24
Battles 296 34
Violence against civilians 297 33

  dimension_variables$dimension,

    dimension_map <- townships_proj %>%
      left_join(
        dimension_gistar %>%
          filter(dimension == current_dimension) %>%
          select(TS_PCODE, hotspot_status),
        by = "TS_PCODE"

The same red symbol now has one meaning in every panel: a significant positive local Gi* under Queen contiguity. The comparison therefore reveals conflict composition rather than a change in mapping rules.

7.5 Monthly hot spot progression

The overall map compresses 57 months into one total. To reveal movement hidden by that aggregation, the next analysis computes Local Gi* separately for every month. It combines the Chapter 10 HCSA map workflow with the Chapter 6 monthly small-multiple layout. Queen contiguity preserves immediate township adjacency and avoids the broad smoothing created by Myanmar’s large critical distance.

Show code 
set.seed(626)

conflict_nb <- conflict_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(
    nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
    wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W", allow_zero = TRUE),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")

gi_stars <- conflict_nb %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  mutate(
    gi_star = local_gstar_perm(
      event_count,
      nb,
      wt,
      nsim = 99,
      zero.policy = TRUE
    )
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(gi_star) %>%
  mutate(
    p_sim_fdr = p.adjust(p_sim, method = "BH"),
    monthly_hotspot = factor(
      if_else(p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0, "Hot spot", "Not a hot spot"),
      levels = c("Not a hot spot", "Hot spot")
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    township_months = n(),
    nominal_hotspot_months = sum(monthly_hotspot == "Hot spot"),
    fdr_significant_months = sum(p_sim_fdr < 0.05 & gi_star > 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  kable()
township_months nominal_hotspot_months fdr_significant_months
18810 1057 0

The same permutation-resolution constraint applies within each monthly slice. The nominal monthly classes support the course EHSA workflow; the zero monthly BH count is not interpreted as proof that spatial concentration is absent.

7.5.1 Latest 12-month HCSA comparison (value-added analysis)

The panels cover the final complete 12-month window, October 2024 to September 2025. Every panel uses the same decision rule and colour scale, so changes in red areas represent changes in significant high-value clustering rather than changes in classification or legend.

Show code 
latest_12_months <- gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(month >= as.Date("2024-10-01")) %>%
  mutate(
    month_label = factor(
      format(month, "%b %Y"),
      levels = format(sort(unique(month)), "%b %Y")
    )
  )

latest_hotspot_persistence <- latest_12_months %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) %>%
  summarise(
    hotspot_months = sum(monthly_hotspot == "Hot spot"),
    events = sum(event_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(hotspot_months > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(hotspot_months), desc(events))

latest_months <- sort(unique(latest_12_months$month))

monthly_hotspot_maps <- map2(
  latest_months,
  seq_along(latest_months),
  function(current_month, map_index) {
    month_map <- townships_proj %>%
      left_join(
        latest_12_months %>%
          filter(month == current_month) %>%
          select(TS_PCODE, monthly_hotspot),
        by = "TS_PCODE"
      )

    tm_shape(month_map) +
      tm_polygons(
        "monthly_hotspot",
        fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
          values = c("grey90", "#D7301F")
        ),
        fill.legend = tm_legend(
          title = "Hot spot status",
          show = map_index == 1,
          position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom")
        )
      ) +
      tm_borders(col = "grey65", lwd = 0.25) +
      tm_shape(states_proj) +
      tm_borders(col = "grey35", lwd = 0.55) +
      tm_title(format(current_month, "%b %Y"))
  }
)

do.call(
  tmap_arrange,
  c(monthly_hotspot_maps, list(ncol = 3, nrow = 4))
)

7.5.2 Hot spot frequency through time

Show code 
monthly_hotspot_counts <- gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(
    hotspot_townships = sum(monthly_hotspot == "Hot spot"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(monthly_hotspot_counts, aes(month, hotspot_townships)) +
  geom_area(fill = "#FCAE91", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_line(colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = "#B2182B", size = 1.2) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks()) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of significant conflict hot-spot townships by month",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Hot-spot townships"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
TipMy observation

Across the latest 12 months, 60 townships appear as a significant hot spot at least once and 8 appear in at least half of the panels. The most frequently repeated locations are Salingyi, Monywa, Pale, Singu, Pakokku. From October 2024 to March 2025, the main concentration stays in the Sagaing-Magway dry-zone corridor: Sagaing leads in October-November and February-March, while Magway is strongest in December-January. The focus shifts southeast to Kayin in April-May, moves toward Mandalay in June-July, and partly returns to Sagaing-Magway in August. September ends with a smaller, fragmented pattern across Kayin, Mandalay, and Magway. Across the full study period, the widest spread occurs in April 2023, with 30 significant hot-spot townships. This sequence provides the transition from overall Local Gi* to the formal EHSA classification.

8 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

8.1 Monthly Gi* values

The next step follows Chapter 11 and In-class Exercise 6. EHSA evaluates the monthly Gi* sequence already visualised above and classifies how each township’s hot-spot behaviour changes through time. The same Queen neighbours and row-standardised weights are passed explicitly into EHSA, keeping the visual diagnosis and formal classification within one spatial model.

NoteResearch link

The monthly Gi* table is the bridge between Chapter 10 and Chapter 11. The spatial weights stay tied to the township layer, while the event count changes by month. This keeps the spatial and temporal dimensions explicit, consistent with the space-time cube approach described by Kim and Lee (2023).

8.2 Mann-Kendall trend check

Show code 
ehsa_mk <- gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(TS_PCODE, TS) %>%
  summarise(
    mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)

ehsa_mk %>%
  arrange(sl, desc(abs(tau))) %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable(digits = 4)
TS_PCODE TS tau sl S D varS
MMR010019 Natogyi 0.6429 0 1026 1596 21102.67
MMR008010 Okpho 0.6416 0 1024 1596 21102.67
MMR006006 Kyunsu 0.6178 0 986 1596 21102.67
MMR012011 Kyaukpyu 0.6065 0 968 1596 21102.67
MMR008009 Minhla 0.6053 0 966 1596 21102.67
MMR006010 Bokpyin 0.6028 0 962 1596 21102.67
MMR008014 Gyobingauk 0.6015 0 960 1596 21102.67
MMR010009 Madaya 0.5940 0 948 1596 21102.67
MMR010018 Taungtha 0.5727 0 914 1596 21102.67
MMR012013 Ramree 0.5714 0 912 1596 21102.67

The Mann-Kendall test evaluates whether the local Gi* sequence has a monotonic trend. A small p-value indicates evidence of change in the Gi* series, while the sign of tau indicates the direction.

TipMy observation

The Mann-Kendall table is a trend check, not a replacement for EHSA. A positive tau means the local Gi* sequence tends to rise, while a negative tau means it tends to fall. The direction alone is not enough; I only treat it as supporting evidence when the trend p-value is small and the EHSA class tells a compatible story.

8.3 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis classification

Show code 
set.seed(626)

ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(
  x = conflict_nb,
  .var = "event_count",
  k = 1,
  nb_col = "nb",
  wt_col = "wt",
  nsim = 99,
  threshold = 0.05
) %>%
  mutate(
    classification = str_replace(
      classification,
      "^oscilating",
      "oscillating"
    ),
    p_value_fdr = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  )

ehsa_hot <- ehsa %>%
  filter(str_detect(classification, regex("hotspot", ignore_case = TRUE)))

ehsa_hot_sig <- ehsa_hot %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05)

ehsa_hot_summary <- ehsa_hot_sig %>%
  count(classification, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

kable(ehsa_hot_summary, digits = 3)

oscillating hotspot 13 0.382
sporadic hotspot 11 0.324
intensifying hotspot 7 0.206
diminishing hotspot 3 0.088

8.3.1 How to read the hot-spot types

EHSA type Temporal meaning
New hotspot The final month is a significant hot spot and the earlier months do not establish a previous hot-spot pattern.
Consecutive hotspot The final months form an uninterrupted hot-spot run, while fewer than 90% of all months are hot spots.
Intensifying hotspot At least 90% of months are hot spots and the Gi* scores show a significant upward trend.
Persistent hotspot At least 90% of months are hot spots without a significant upward or downward trend.
Diminishing hotspot At least 90% of months are hot spots and the Gi* scores show a significant downward trend.
Sporadic hotspot Hot-spot months occur intermittently, covering fewer than 90% of the series, without an opposing significant pattern.
Oscillating hotspot The final month is a hot spot and earlier months contain an opposing significant pattern, indicating temporal reversal.
Historical hotspot Earlier months establish a sustained hot-spot pattern, while the recent period no longer does so.

These definitions turn the EHSA map into a temporal reading: location answers where, the class answers how the pattern evolved, and the monthly profile shows the evidence behind that summary.

Show code 
ehsa_map <- townships_proj %>%
  left_join(ehsa_hot_sig, by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location"))

ehsa_sig <- ehsa_map %>%
  filter(!is.na(classification))

tm_shape(ehsa_map) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "grey90",
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Not significant")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(ehsa_sig) +
  tm_polygons(
    "classification",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = "brewer.set3"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "EHSA class")
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey30", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(states_proj) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey20", lwd = 0.9) +
  tm_title("Significant emerging hot spot classes (p < 0.05)")

The EHSA map shows only significant hot-spot classifications over a full township background. The four observed significant classes have different spatial and temporal meanings.

8.3.2 Intensifying hotspots

Seven intensifying hotspots form the clearest upward-priority group. Muse, Namhkan, and Namhsan place three of them in northern Shan, while Kyethi and Mongpan extend the pattern into southern Shan. Kawthoung represents a separate far-southern concentration and Dagon Myothit (North) an urban Yangon case. Their positive Mann-Kendall tau values indicate that local Gi* scores have tended to rise through the 57-month sequence. The geographical separation shows that intensification is not one continuous national corridor; it appears in several conflict theatres.

8.3.3 Oscillating hotspots

Thirteen oscillating hotspots are distributed across Kachin, Mandalay, Rakhine, Bago, Magway, Shan, Ayeyarwady, and Nay Pyi Taw. Kachin contributes Hpakant, Injangyang, and Shwegu; Mandalay contributes Sintgaing and Tada-U; Rakhine contributes Rathedaung and Mrauk-U. Their sequences alternate between hotspot and opposing or non-hotspot conditions. They indicate recurring spatial reversals rather than a stable escalation path, so current field verification matters more than a single long-run ranking.

8.3.4 Sporadic hotspots

Eleven sporadic hotspots are geographically dispersed. Bago contributes Phyu, Taungoo, Padaung, and Minhla; Mandalay contributes Madaya and Amarapura; southern Shan contributes Laihka and Nansang. Khaunglanhpu, Mese, and Launglon form isolated cases in Kachin, Kayah, and Tanintharyi. Their separated significant months support flexible monitoring because the concentration reappears without forming one continuous temporal run.

8.3.5 Diminishing hotspots

Chipwi and Myitkyina in Kachin and Pyay in Bago (West) are significant diminishing hotspots. Their negative Mann-Kendall tau values show a downward trend in local Gi* intensity after substantial earlier hotspot presence. Diminishing describes the direction of the spatial statistic; it does not establish conflict resolution or the absence of present-day risk.

8.4 Representative temporal profiles

The class map summarises 57 monthly values into one label per township. The following profiles restore that temporal detail. One high-event township is selected from each observed hot-spot class, allowing the class definitions to be compared with the underlying Gi* paths.

Show code 
representative_hotspots <- ehsa_hot_sig %>%
  left_join(
    township_totals %>%
      st_drop_geometry() %>%
      select(TS_PCODE, TS, event_count),
    by = c("location" = "TS_PCODE")
  ) %>%
  group_by(classification) %>%
  slice_max(event_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

hotspot_profiles <- gi_stars %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  inner_join(
    representative_hotspots %>%
      select(location, classification),
    by = c("TS_PCODE" = "location")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    profile = paste(TS, classification, sep = ": "),
    significant_hotspot = p_sim < 0.05 & gi_star > 0
  )

ggplot(hotspot_profiles, aes(month, gi_star)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_point(
    aes(colour = significant_hotspot),
    size = 1.5
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "#B2182B"),
    labels = c(`FALSE` = "Other month", `TRUE` = "Significant hot spot"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  facet_wrap(vars(profile), ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Gi* profiles for representative emerging hot spots",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Local Gi* score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Red points identify months with statistically significant positive Gi*. Consecutive red points indicate sustained episodes, separated red points indicate intermittent concentration, and a late run of red points provides the visual signature expected for a recent or intensifying pattern. The Mann-Kendall result adds the formal monotonic-trend evidence used by EHSA.

TipMy observation

The class table establishes whether the significant result is dominated by repeated, intermittent, or changing high-value concentration. The 12-month maps show the latest geographical sequence, while the representative profiles expose the full monthly trajectories behind selected class labels. The BH-adjusted count is retained as a multiple-testing sensitivity check. The map follows the assignment’s required nominal p < 0.05 threshold, while the stricter count shows how much evidence remains after controlling the false discovery rate.

9 Integrated findings

Evidence layer Core finding What it adds
Conflict dimensions 19 townships are hotspots across all three variables; battle-led and civilian-harm hotspots reveal different conflict compositions. The aggregate map is a shared baseline, not a substitute for conflict-specific inference.
Local association LISA identifies 34 High-High clusters and 4 Low-High outliers; fixed-distance Gi* identifies 78 hotspots. Clusters, outliers, and high-value concentrations answer distinct spatial questions.
Monthly movement The widest spread occurs in April 2023, with 30 hotspot townships. Concentration moves from the dry zone toward Kayin and Mandalay before partially returning.
Emerging patterns Significant EHSA results comprise 13 oscillating hotspot, 11 sporadic hotspot, 7 intensifying hotspot, 3 diminishing hotspot. The same red hotspot symbol can represent escalation, recurrence, intermittence, or decline.

The evidence becomes more specific at each stage: burden, local association, monthly movement, then temporal trajectory. Every result describes recorded concentration rather than the cause of violence.

NoteResearch reading

This pattern is consistent with the purpose of EHSA in Chapter 11: it separates repeated temporal behaviour from one-period spikes. The monthly small multiples apply the comparative display logic in Chapter 6 to the HCSA classes derived in Chapter 10. It also matches the caution in conflict point-pattern research that observed event concentration should be read as a spatio-temporal pattern, not an automatic causal explanation (Mack and Kam, 2018).

10 Peace-building implications

Hotspot signal Planning response Reason
Repeated in recent monthly panels Sustained township-level review Concentration recurs rather than appearing in one isolated month.
Intensifying Current field verification and closer monitoring Local Gi* strength is rising through the study period.
Sporadic or oscillating Flexible, event-triggered monitoring Significant concentration disappears and returns or reverses.
Diminishing Follow-up before de-prioritisation Declining relative concentration does not demonstrate low present-day harm.

These maps are a prioritisation screen. Decisions still require current access conditions, displacement and population exposure, and consultation with affected communities.

10.1 Limitations

Constraint Consequence Treatment in this report
ACLED reporting coverage Recorded events may vary with access and source availability. Results are described as recorded concentration.
Township and monthly aggregation Boundaries and time bins shape the clusters; within-month order disappears. Claims stay at township-month scale.
Event counts High burden is not the same as high population risk. Implications require exposure and displacement evidence.
99 permutations Simulated p-values cannot fall below about 0.01, limiting BH resolution across 330 tests. Nominal results follow the course workflow; BH counts are shown as a stricter check.
Spatial support The 185.8 km fixed band smooths broadly; Queen weights follow immediate adjacency and contain disconnected components. Each weight is tied to its stated analytical question.
Twelve-panel display The visual window covers October 2024 to September 2025. EHSA classification still uses the complete 57-month sequence.
